So. You've heard what the treaty costs. Now here's what it buys.

{{< var diseases_without_effective_treatment >}} have zero approved treatments. Not "in development." Not "awaiting funding." Zero. If you're diagnosed with one of them today, your treatment does not exist. At the rate of {{< var current_drug_approvals_per_year >}} new approvals per year, the queue clears in roughly {{< var status_quo_queue_clearance_years >}}. That is not a timeline. That is a rejection letter written in slow motion.

The system isn't broken. It was never built. What exists is a regulatory obstacle course that costs {{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}} per patient. That's a Tesla. Per person. To find out if a pill works. The pill costs 37 cents to make. The paperwork weighs more than the patient.

## What a Fix Actually Costs

![It'll cost 40 million to run this per year. Maybe 27 million, maybe 56 million. Either way, less than one fighter jet.](/assets/images/health-dividend/health-dividend-section-the-framework-cost-breakdown-bw-academic.jpg)

Your decentralized FDA costs {{< var dfda_annual_opex >}} per year to operate. Servers, engineers, compliance, global integration. The boring stuff that saves billions.

For context, this is roughly what your species spends annually on Halloween costumes for dogs. Less than one fighter jet. Less than one yacht. Less than what FIFA spends on "hospitality." I need you to sit with that for a moment.

## Why Your Trials Cost a Tesla Per Person

Traditional Phase III trials cost **{{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}}** per patient. Then the Oxford RECOVERY trial proved you can do the same thing for **{{< var recovery_trial_cost_per_patient >}}**. During a pandemic. While panicking. They tested COVID treatments on 40,000+ patients by using existing hospital staff (revolutionary concept: doctors treating patients), collecting data electronically instead of sacrificing forests to the paperwork gods, and focusing on what actually matters: does the patient live or die? Not "did they complete form 27-B in triplicate?"

Scale that model globally and you get up to **{{< var dfda_trial_cost_reduction_factor >}} cost reduction**. Same data quality. Better real-world applicability. It turns out you don't need 17 committees to answer the question "did the medicine work?"

Your species spends **{{< var global_clinical_trials_spending_annual >}} per year** on clinical trials, and growing, because apparently inefficiency scales beautifully. Cut {{< var dfda_trial_cost_reduction_pct >}} of that waste and you save **{{< var dfda_benefit_rd_only_annual >}} annually** [@industry-clinical-trial-spending-estimate]. That's the savings from making trials less stupid. We haven't even counted the lives yet.

## What Changes for the Human Who Gets Sick

![With 58.6 billion, you could run 10,000 trials and address 7,000 rare diseases. Currently you're spending that much to run far fewer trials for common diseases. Priorities.](/assets/images/health-dividend/health-dividend-section-what-var-dfda-benefit-rd-only-annual-buys-you-bw-academic.jpg)

This is the part that matters. Right now, if you're diagnosed with one of those {{< var rare_diseases_count_global_nounit >}} untreated diseases, you enter a waiting room. The waiting room has no exit date. The humans in it die there. Not because a cure is impossible, but because nobody funded the trial.

Each new drug approval is worth an average of $1.62 billion [@arxiv-2212-07384] in market value. The FDA approves roughly {{< var current_drug_approvals_per_year >}}. That is the speed at which a species with nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence has chosen to cure itself. Staggering.

With {{< var dfda_trial_capacity_multiplier >}} more trial capacity, you could fund **10,000 new pragmatic clinical trials** every year at $5M each (still luxurious by RECOVERY standards). You could test treatments for **{{< var rare_diseases_count_global_nounit >}} rare diseases** currently ignored because orphan diseases aren't profitable enough for your orphan-making economic system. You could cut drug development time from 17 years to 3-5 years, because most terminal patients don't have 17 years, and this has not occurred to anyone in charge. You could make medicines affordable by eliminating {{< var pharma_drug_development_cost_current >}} development costs (roughly 90% of which is lawyers arguing about commas).

That waiting room? It empties. Your treatment arrives in your lifetime instead of centuries after your death.

## The Cost of Taking Your Time

Disease costs humanity **$397.4 trillion annually** [@disease-economic-burden-109t]. That's more than global GDP ($101 trillion [@global-gdp]). The number sounds wrong because your economists spent centuries measuring productivity without accounting for the humans who stopped being productive on account of being dead. The missing piece is DALYs (Disability-Adjusted Life Years): healthy years deleted by disease. Globally, that's **{{< var global_annual_daly_burden_nounit >}} DALYs annually** [@ihme-gbd-2021].

Every day without this system costs **{{< var dfda_rd_savings_daily >}}** in wasted trial spending alone. Delayed treatments cost {{< var dfda_efficacy_lag_elimination_dalys >}} healthy life-years over the full lag period (cumulative across all deaths and disability during the delay, not a single year's burden). The regulatory lag period is not a safety feature. It is a waiting room where people die. You just gave the waiting room a nicer name.

See [Daily Opportunity Cost of Inaction](https://dfda-impact.warondisease.org#daily-opportunity-cost-of-inaction) for calculations.

## The Return

![Conservative return on investment versus total return including not letting people die. One number is big, the other is astronomically big. Both beat war.](/assets/images/health-dividend/health-dividend-section-roi-scenarios-bw-academic.jpg)

Your decentralized FDA costs {{< var dfda_annual_opex >}} per year to run. It saves {{< var dfda_benefit_rd_only_annual >}} per year in clinical trial waste. That's **{{< var dfda_roi_rd_only >}}:1** returns on R&D savings alone, without counting a single life saved. Include the lives, and the total societal benefit hits **{{< var treaty_roi_trial_capacity_plus_efficacy_lag >}}:1**.

Even the worst case, where everything goes wrong, adoption is terrible, the engineers quit and the servers catch fire, still returns an estimated 66:1. That beats every military investment in human history. Your worst medical outcome is still better than your best military one. Let that sink in while you're approving next year's defense budget.
